diagnosis: Don at Parkhill, calibrated with DDS on daily NSE over 1971-10 to 1997-12. The first year was used as warm-up, and initial soil storage was set near its long-term mean. Calibration NSE is 0.824, KGE 0.873, PBIAS +1.9% and r 0.91. Two independent DDS searches with different seeds and starting points both converged to NSE of about 0.823. They found similar values for FC (335-377 mm), LP (0.9-0.97), BETA (3-4), K1 (about 0.2), K2 (about 0.06), PERC (about 4), MAXBAS (about 2.5), TT (about 0.27), CFMAX (about 2) and SFCF (about 0.9). Most parameters are therefore well identified. K0 and UZL are poorly identified: the two searches gave K0 of 0.21 vs 0.99 and UZL of 23 vs 42 with almost the same score, so quick-flow peaks are weakly constrained. The snow liquid-water parameters CWH and CFR ended near zero and matter little, since only about 6% of precipitation falls as snow. Likely weaknesses: underestimated flood peaks from convective or high-intensity storms, timing errors in winter snowmelt from the higher Cairngorm headwaters, and low-flow recession in dry summers. The fairly fast baseflow (K2 of about 0.06) fits a catchment with little productive aquifer. No split-sample validation was run. Because the parameters are stable across searches, I expect performance in 1998-2008 to be similar, with NSE of roughly 0.78-0.82.

diagnosis: I calibrated HBV on daily NSE over 1971-10 to 1997-12 using the global DDS optimiser, run twice from different starting points and seeds. Both runs reached the same ceiling: NSE 0.646 and 0.648, KGE about 0.77, r 0.81. The run I submit has a bias of -3%, so the water balance is about right. Fit is only moderate for an upland catchment. The likely reason is that a single lumped snow routine with one temperature series cannot represent snow across 70–1309 m. The optimiser compensates with a high snow threshold (TT about 1.2 °C), reduced snowfall (SFCF about 0.73), fast melt (CFMAX about 5.6) and almost no refreezing or retained meltwater (CFR and CWH at their lower bounds). Spring melt timing and rain-on-snow peaks are probably the weakest periods, along with the very large flood peaks. Simulated maximum flow is about 24 mm/d against 33 mm/d observed. Confidence: the snow and water-balance parameters (TT, CFMAX, SFCF, PERC about 4.5, K2 about 0.05) came out almost the same in both runs. The fast-response and soil parameters (K0, UZL, LP, BETA, FC from 145 to 190 mm) differ a lot between equally good runs. Both runs pinned some parameters to their range limits, and I did not widen those ranges and recalibrate. I also did no split-sample check, so the expected NSE in 1998–2008 is roughly 0.6–0.65, untested.

diagnosis: I calibrated against daily NSE over 1971-10 to 1997-12 after a one-year warm-up, using DDS from the default parameters followed by a Nelder-Mead polish. The fit is moderate: NSE 0.65, KGE 0.78, r 0.81 and a bias of about -4%. A second independent DDS search reached nearly the same parameter set and NSE 0.644, so the optimum looks stable. The final parameters are: TT about 1.2 °C, CFMAX 5.6, SFCF 0.71, FC about 228 mm, LP about 1.0, BETA 1.2, K1 0.42, K2 0.064, PERC 6.9 and MAXBAS 2.2. Fast reservoirs and a short routing time fit a steep upland catchment with thin soils and little groundwater storage. I did not test the parameters on a held-out period. The main weakness is likely snow. With one temperature series for terrain from 70 to 1300 m, the model handles snow accumulation and melt in the Cairngorms poorly. The low snowfall correction (SFCF), high threshold temperature (TT) and near-zero values for liquid water retention in snow (CWH) and refreezing (CFR) are partly compensating for this. Peak flows from winter rain-on-snow and spring melt are probably simulated poorly, and some flood peaks are underestimated. I am fairly confident in the response and soil parameters but less so in the snow parameters. I expect NSE in the later period to be similar, roughly 0.6 to 0.65.

diagnosis: I calibrated the model with DDS on daily NSE over 1971–1997, after a one-year warm-up. The best set reached NSE 0.648, KGE 0.78 and r 0.81, with a volume bias of about −5%. I ran the same parameter set alone over 1987–1997, a window that falls inside the calibration period, so it is not an independent check; it gave NSE 0.655. Two independent DDS searches converged to about the same NSE (0.646 and 0.648) with quite different response and soil parameters (for example K0 0.99 vs 0.14 and LP 0.56 vs 0.97). This equifinality means the individual parameters are uncertain, although the simulated hydrographs perform alike. The fit levels off at an NSE around 0.65, which points to errors in the inputs or model structure rather than to the optimiser. Likely causes are snowmelt and rain-on-snow in the high Cairngorm headwaters (lumped temperature with a single TT), how much rain lands on the upland areas, and timing errors in flood peaks. The snow parameters (TT about 1.0 °C, CFMAX about 5, SFCF about 0.7, which reduces snowfall) take up some of this input bias. The volume bias in 1987–1997 was larger (about −10%). Weak points: the residual errors are probably largest at storm peaks (convective summer events and the largest winter floods), and the single lower store may simplify summer low-flow recessions. On this fairly permeable arable catchment, groundwater from the sand and gravel aquifers likely adds slow baseflow that one store can't fully represent. CWH ended at its lower bound, but it has almost no effect here. I'm fairly confident in the soil and response parameters, which are well constrained by 26 years of data. The snow parameters are poorly identified. I expect the 1998–2008 NSE to be slightly lower, around 0.80–0.85.

diagnosis: I calibrated the model to daily NSE over all of 1971-10 to 1997-12 using DDS: 3000 runs, then two refinement rounds of 1500 runs each. Before the last round I set the starting soil and groundwater stores (soil moisture 170 mm, lower store 40 mm, upper store 2 mm) close to their usual levels. The fit is good: NSE 0.875, KGE 0.925, a small overestimate of volume (PBIAS -2.5%) and r 0.936. As a check, I reran the same parameters on 1986-1997 alone, which gave NSE 0.887. This is not an independent test, because those years were also used in calibration, but it suggests the fit is stable over time. The parameters look reasonable for a wet, steep Scottish upland catchment: FC about 186 mm, LP about 1.0 (at the top of its range), a fairly linear soil response (BETA 1.3), fast upper-zone runoff (K1 0.19, K0 0.87, UZL 66 mm), high percolation (PERC 6.9) into a moderately responsive groundwater store (K2 0.064), and a short routing delay (MAXBAS 2.9 days). Snow plays a small role: TT about 0.9 °C, CFMAX 4.4 and snowfall correction 0.81. CFR and CWH end up near zero and have little effect. Weak spots: the highest peaks are underestimated (simulated maximum about 28 vs 37 mm/d observed). Regulation by the catchment's 16 reservoirs and hydropower schemes, and errors in snowmelt timing, are not represented. Several parameters, especially the snow parameters and the K0/UZL/PERC trade-offs, are likely interchangeable without changing the fit much. My confidence in the overall simulated flows is moderate to high; my confidence in individual parameter values is lower.

tools: calibrate:4 clone_model:3 create_model:2 get_parameter_ranges:1 load_data:4 run_model:5 set_parameter_ranges:2 set_parameters:4 submit_calibration:1
diagnosis:
I'm submitting model-3, calibrated with DDS (NSE objective) on 1986-1997 after a one-year warm-up, starting from the default store levels. Its daily NSE is 0.68 with PBIAS -3% in that period. Restarted from the same default levels on 1971-1985, the same parameters give NSE 0.62 with PBIAS -1%. Run continuously over all of 1971-1997, they give NSE 0.61 with PBIAS +19%.

The catchment does not close its water balance. Mean flow is about 2.6 mm/d against 5.7 mm/d of rain and 1.1 mm/d of potential evaporation, probably because the Loch Lyon / Breadalbane hydropower scheme moves water out of the catchment. HBV has no proper loss term, so the calibration fakes one in three ways: the snow correction factor sits at its minimum of 0.4, soil capacity (FC) is very large at about 780 mm, and the lower groundwater store keeps filling during the run and drains very slowly (K2 about 3e-4). Two attempts at a steadier loss scored worse (NSE 0.59).

Because that store keeps filling, results depend on how long the run is and where it starts. A short run from default store levels should behave like these tests (NSE about 0.62-0.68). A run started in 1970 would drift towards too much flow. Peaks and low flows that are set by the regulated reservoirs are reproduced poorly. Confidence in the individual parameters is low, because they mostly make up for the diversion rather than describe real catchment behaviour.

tools: calibrate:4 clone_model:2 create_model:1 get_parameter_ranges:1 load_data:2 run_model:5 set_initial_conditions:4 set_parameter_ranges:3 set_parameters:1 submit_calibration:1
diagnosis: Calibration NSE is 0.68 (KGE 0.78, PBIAS about 0%) for 1971–1997. On 1989–1997, run as a separate check, NSE is 0.69 and PBIAS is -1%, so performance looks stable over time. This is a regulated catchment: the Loch Lyon and Loch an Daimh hydro reservoirs divert water. Observed runoff (about 2.65 mm/d) is far below precipitation minus PET (about 4.6 mm/d), so the standard HBV water balance cannot close. I closed it with two non-physical choices. First, PERC (about 6.7 mm/d) drains the upper zone into a lower store that acts as a near-permanent sink (K2 = 1e-6). This mimics the hydro intakes capturing flow up to a capacity limit. Second, that lower store starts at 1e6 mm, so it releases an almost constant baseflow of about 1 mm/d, standing in for compensation flows. Its level drifted only about 1% over 27 years, so the setup does not change over time. SFCF (about 0.4) also removes some snow water. Weaknesses: floods are smoothed by the reservoirs and diversions, so peaks are underestimated (simulated maximum 42 vs 60 mm/d observed). Low flows are simulated as a flat constant. Snow and the soil parameters (FC about 790, BETA about 0.5) are only loosely identifiable. I trust the water balance and the stable timing, but the parameters are compensating for missing regulation processes, so the individual values have little physical meaning.

diagnosis: Lyon at Comrie Bridge has hydropower abstractions (the Loch Lyon / Breadalbane scheme). Observed runoff is only about 45% of precipitation, and evapotranspiration cannot explain the gap, so HBV has to lose water another way. The best fits do this in two ways. First, a low SFCF (~0.41) with TT ~1.3 removes part of the snowfall. Second, high PERC (~6 mm/d) feeds a lower store that drains very slowly (K2 ~2.4e-4), so the store behaves as a sink. Fast runoff is handled by the upper zone (K0 0.19, K1 0.24, UZL 28) with short routing (MAXBAS ~1.3). Because K2 is so small, the lower store keeps filling over a ~11-year run, so the water loss in the model changes over time. I calibrated the parameters with a fresh start (default initial stores) on an 11-year window (1986–97), matching the length of the scoring period. NSE was 0.68 on that window and 0.63 in an independent fresh-start test on 1971–82, with volume bias of -6% and -12%. Main weaknesses: large flood peaks are underestimated (earlier 1970s), baseflow is poorly represented, and flow released from the reservoirs is not modelled. The parameters are not physically meaningful (snow and soil values are at or near their bounds). If the scoring run starts from much fuller stores, flows would be overestimated. Confidence is moderate: expected NSE is about 0.6–0.68.
